fullText: Pearl High School. The Pearl High School shooting is often overshadowed by Coline and others, but it was one of the earliest school shootings that helped shape America's late 1990s school violence crisis. On October 1, 1997, 16-year-old Luke Woodham targeted his mother, Maryanne Woodham, as she prepared for her morning job. Armed with a baseball bat and a knife, he brutally attacked her inside their home. At 8:06 a.m., Woodham arrived at Pearl High School wearing a trench coat to conceal a 3030 hunting rifle. Moments before opening fire, he handed his manifesto to a friend, Justin Sledge. He then entered the crowded commons area. Woodham opened fire on his ex-girlfriend, Christine Mini, 16, and Lydia Dub, 17. Both were killed. He continued firing into the crowd, wounding seven more students as terrified teenagers ran for cover. Assistant Principal Joe Mirk retrieved a 45 caliber pistol from his truck and confronted Woodham as he attempted to flee the campus. Mirik held Wood at gunpoint until police arrived, preventing any further attacks. Investigators later discovered that Woodham may have intended to continue the rampage at another nearby school. Before the massacre, Woodham had written Stranger Things in class, expressed thoughts of ending his life after his breakup with Minifi, and threatened her. Months earlier, he and associates had tortured and killed his pet dog, Sparkle, which he described in his writings as his first successful kill. Woodam was ultimately convicted and sentenced to three consecutive life terms, plus 140 years in prison. The Pearl shooting remains one of the most significant yet often forgotten school shootings in American history. University of Texas Tower. On August 1st, 1966, one of the earliest and most shocking mass shootings in American history unfolded at the University of Texas at Austin. At midnight, 25-year-old Charles Whitman drove to his mother's apartment and fatally stabbed her while she slept, leaving a note. Around 3:00 a.m., Whitman returned home and stabbed his wife to death in a similar manner. again leaving a note describing affection, confusion, and violent thoughts. Later that morning, he withdrew money, purchased multiple firearms, and hundreds of rounds of ammunition from several stores, and modified a shotgun by sawing off its barrel. He packed his weapon, supplies, and food into a large foot locker. Disguised in workclo to appear as a maintenance worker, he drove to the University of Texas campus shortly before noon. At approximately 11:30 a.m., Whitman entered the university's main building, incapacitated a receptionist, and erected a makeshift barricade. He then killed someone at close range before moving on to the observation deck. At 11:48 a.m., women began firing from the tower 231 ft above the ground. For the next 96 minutes, he shot at people across the campus and surrounding streets, killing students, staff, and civilians at distances of up to several hundred yards. Many initially mistook the gunfire for construction noise, delaying the realization of an active attack. Officers and armed civilians returned fire from the ground, forcing Whitman to stay low. Eventually, multiple officers ascended the tower. At approximately 1:24 p.m., two Austin police officers confronted Whitman on the observation deck and fatally shot him at close range. By the time the shooting ended, Whitman had killed 14 people and wounded more than 30 others. After the investigation, the main motive of the perpetrator was believed to be his psychological issues. following his parents' divorce. This was considered one of the most horrific shooting incidents in US history. [clears throat] Bath school. The Bath School disaster is known as the worst school shooting in history in the United States. It took place on May 18th, 1927 in Ba Township. The attacker, Andrew Kho, a 55-year-old farmer and schoolboard treasurer, had spent months secretly preparing his plan. Angry over rising taxes and personal failures, he used his access to the school to plant over a ton of dynamite and pyol beneath the building. At 8:45 a.m., Kiho set fire to his own farm, destroying his property after murdering his wife, Nelly. While the town was distracted by the fire, the real tragedy began. At 9:45 a.m., a timed explosive detonated beneath the north wing of the school. The building collapsed instantly, killing students and teachers where they stood. Students were thrown from windows and buried under rubble. Survivors screamed from beneath the debris. Rescuers rushed in, many coming directly from the burning farm. But about 30 minutes later, Kiho returned in a truck filled with explosives and metal fragments. He parked near the damaged school and called over Superintendent Emory Huk. Moments later, Kiho detonated the truck, killing himself, Hiuk, and several others. The blast sent shrapnel flying across the area, injuring more rescuers. When it was over, 45 people were dead, including 38 students. Nellie's body was later found hidden on the farm. Investigators later found another 500 lb of explosives under the south wing that failed to detonate. EL poly techchnique de Montreal. This was one of the deadliest and most notorious school shootings in Canadian history. Yet many people have never heard of it. On December 6th, 1989, at approximately 5:10 p.m., 25-year-old Mark Lepin entered the Equil Poly Techchnique Engineering School armed with a Ruger Mini-14 semi-automatic rifle and a hunting knife. He walked into a mechanical engineering classroom on the second floor and ordered everyone to stop what they were doing. Leine then separated the students by sex, forcing about 50 male students to leave the room while nine female students remained. When questioned about what he was doing, he declared he was fighting feminism. 6 seconds later, he opened fire on the women, shooting from left to right. Six women were killed and three others were wounded. Nepine then left the classroom and continued his attack throughout the building, moving through hallways, stairwells, the cafeteria, and additional classrooms. He specifically targeted women. In the cafeteria, he murdered two women who were attempting to hide. on the third floor. He shot several more female students. He stabbed a wounded student before turning the gun on himself. The entire attack lasted about 20 minutes. 14 women had been murdered, including 12 engineering students, one nursing student, and a university employee. 14 other people were injured. Investigators later discovered a three-page suicide letter in which Leine blamed feminists for ruining his life. The letter also contained a list of 19 prominent Quebec women he claimed he wanted to kill. He had legally purchased the rifle weeks earlier and had been seen around the campus multiple times before the attack. Marjgery Stoneman Douglas High School. One afternoon on February 14th, 2018, a student appeared at Marjgery Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, armed with a semi-automatic rifle and multiple magazines. At approximately 2:21 p.m., he quickly assembled his weapon at the base of a stairwell and told student Christopher McKenna, who accidentally walked by, "You'd better get out of here." As he entered the first floor hallway, he fatally shot three students. The attacker then fired through the windows of four closed classroom doors on the other side of the hallway, killing six more students and wounding 13 others on the first floor of the building. As the fire alarm sounded, students panicked and evacuated into hallways rather than sheltering in place. After moving through all three floors of the building and expending large amounts of ammunition, the gunman stopped shooting, abandoned his weapon, and escaped the scene by blending in with fleeing students. The attack resulted in 17 people being killed and 18 more being wounded. At about 3:41 p.m., police arrested the suspect without resistance 2 miles from the school. The gunman was Nicholas Cruz, a 19-year-old former student who'd been expelled for disciplinary reasons. Investigators revealed that Cruz had a documented history of behavioral problems, violent threats, and contact with law enforcement. In 2022, Cruz was charged with 17 counts of first-degree murder. As a result, Cruz was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Dunlain Primary School. One of the deadliest school shootings in modern British history happened in a quiet Scottish town. On March 13, 1996, 43-year-old Thomas Hamilton left his home in Sterling and drove to Dunla Primary School. Before entering the campus, he cut nearby telephone cables in an apartment attempting to disrupt emergency communications. Hamilton was armed with four owned handguns, two Browning 9mm pistols, and two Smith and Wesson 357 Magnum revolvers. At around 9:35 a.m., he entered the school through a side entrance. After firing shots into a hallway in a nearby classroom, he made his way to the gymnasium. Inside, a class of 28 students was preparing for a physical education lesson with their teacher, Gwen Mayer, and several staff members. Hamilton immediately opened fire. PE teacher Eileen Harold and assistant Mary Blake tried to shield the children. They were shot and wounded. Teacher Gwen Mayer was killed almost instantly. Hamilton then moved around the gym, firing repeatedly at groups of children who were hiding, wounded, or attempting to escape. Some victims were shot at extremely close range. He briefly fired outside through an emergency exit, injuring staff member Grace Twiddle and shooting toward a nearby portable classroom. He then returned to the gymnasium. Just 3 to 4 minutes after the attack began, Hamilton dropped one of his pistols and used a .357 Magnum revolver to shoot himself dead. The massacre left 16 children and one teacher dead at the scene. Another child died on the way to the hospital, bringing the death toll to 18 victims. 15 others were injured. The tragedy sparked the massive snowdrop petition, which gathered more than 700,000 signatures and led to some of the strictest handgun laws in the world. Future tennis champions Andy Murray and Jamie Murray were students at the school that day and survived the attack. Ufort school 19-year-old Robert Steinhauser had been expelled from Gutenberg Gymnasium in Urfort for forging medical documents and had secretly hidden the expulsion from his parents. On April 26th, 2002, Steinhauser arrived at the school armed with a Glock 17 pistol, a Mossberg shotgun that was unusable due to a technical problem, and a knife. At around 10:45 a.m., he entered the building without a mask, and asked staff whether the principal was present. He then went into a restroom, changed into black clothing resembling a ninja outfit and put on a mask. At 10:58 a.m., the shooting began. Steinhauser first entered the administration area, killing the vice principal and a secretary. He then moved methodically through the school, targeting teachers supervising ambiter examinations. He often stopped outside classrooms and used deception to lure teachers into hallways before shooting them at close range. Students barricaded themselves inside classrooms. Unlike many school shooters, Steinhauser largely ignored students and focused his attack on teachers and school staff, apparently seeking revenge for his expulsion. At 11:12 a.m., police arrived at the scene. From a classroom window, Steinhauser shot and killed a police officer with a single shot to the head. History and art teacher Rainor Heis confronted the gunman in a hallway. Pulling off Steinhauser's mask, he looked him in the eye and said, "Robert, this is enough. If you want, you can shoot me." The gunman lowered his weapon and replied, "Mr. Heis, that's enough for today." He then tricked him into entering room 111 and locked the door from outside. Trapped inside, Steinhauser shot himself. The attack lasted about 20 minutes. By the end, 16 people had been murdered, including 12 teachers, one trainee teacher, one secretary, one police officer, and two students who were struck through a classroom door. Steinhauser was obsessed with violent media and shooting sports and had previously joked about killing a teacher during a school trip. Just days before the attack, his mother discovered ammunition in his room, and the school received a threatening phone call. Winn school. The Winnan school shooting remains one of Europe's deadliest yet often forgotten school attacks. On the morning of March 11th, 2009, 17-year-old Tim Cretchmer, a former student of Albertville Real Shaw in Winnendon, stole a 9mm Beretta pistol from his father's gun collection and entered the school. At approximately 9:30 a.m., dressed in black, he began firing inside the school. Moving through three classrooms and a chemistry laboratory, he shot his students and teachers at close range, often aiming for the head. As the attack unfolded, the principal broadcast a coded warning over the school's loudspeaker system. Mrs. coma is coming," a reference to the German word amuk, meaning a killing frenzy. Police received the first emergency call at 9:33 a.m. and arrived within minutes. Officers encountered Cretchmer on a staircase where he exchanged gunfire with them before fleeing the building. As he escaped, he shot and killed two additional teachers in the hallway. Nine students and three teachers had been murdered inside the school. The gunman fled through a nearby park where he killed a groundskeeper at a psychiatric clinic. Around 10 a.m., he hijacked a minivan and forced the driver to take him roughly 40 kilometers to the town of Wendlingan. At noon, after the driver managed to escape, Gretchmer entered a Volkswagen dealership. There, he shot and killed a salesman and a customer. Police quickly surrounded the area, leading to a violent gun battle that seriously wounded two officers. After being shot in the leg, Cretchmer turned the gun on himself at approximately 12:15 p.m. During the rampage, he fired a total of 112 rounds. Most of his victims were female. Eight of the nine students killed at the school were girls and all three murdered teachers were women. According to the kidnapped driver, when asked why he was doing it, Kretchmer allegedly replied, "Because it's fun." Investigators later discovered that Cretchmer had undergone treatment for depression. He also participated in online discussions about school shootings and had hinted that people often ignore warnings before a massacre occurs.
